routes.description: Establish that theism provides a more adequate unified account of scientific intelligibility, reliable cognition, objective moral obligation, apparent order, and the broader context of suffering than skeptical naturalism provides.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its account connects theism to the principal scientific, epistemic, moral, and explanatory facts while answering naturalistic mechanisms, evidential objections, religious plurality, and the challenge from evil without relying on a merely unexplained gap.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined scientific, moral, and explanatory considerations support theism more strongly than skeptical naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Explain why an orderly and mathematically intelligible universe, truth-directed cognition, and the value of inquiry are expected under a rational creator.
Ground objective moral status and obligation in theism while distinguishing normative authority from evolved feelings or social conditioning.
Defend divine agency as an explanation of established order and functional organization rather than an inference confined to temporary ignorance.
Reconcile suffering with theism or show that the objection requires moral and eschatological premises that the theistic account can coherently supply.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect the historical emergence of modern science to theological commitments about an ordered, knowable, and worthwhile creation.
Specify what observations or comparative explanations may count for theism despite alternative natural or advanced-agent interpretations.

routes.description: Establish that public evidence, testable natural mechanisms, and empirically informed morality explain the relevant phenomena without a divine hypothesis, while suffering and underdetermination count against traditional theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if natural inquiry remains adequate for science, cognition, origins, design, and morality; if proposed divine explanations lack discriminating support or specificity; and if theism does not resolve the evidential challenge posed by innocent suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that the relevant evidence and explanatory methods support skeptical naturalism at least more strongly than the proposed theistic account.

centralBridges.description: Require publicly reproducible, discriminating evidence and causal mechanisms before treating supernatural agency as an explanation.
Account for apparent design, cognitive reliability, and possible cosmic origins through testable or provisionally investigated natural processes.
Explain moral knowledge and obligation through facts about sentient flourishing, reciprocity, cooperation, reasoning, and empirically studied human nature.
Establish the evidential tension between extensive preventable innocent suffering and a deity possessing perfect goodness and unlimited power.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate scientific validity from the religious identity of early investigators and address the specificity problem created by competing religions.
Identify how unfalsifiable qualifications, asymmetric attribution, or appeals to unknown causes limit the explanatory content of the God hypothesis.

sections.title: Scientific Intelligibility, Cognition, and Historical Origins
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the order of nature, human access to truth, the value of inquiry, and the historical rise of science receive a distinctive theistic explanation or are adequately grounded by universal scientific practice and evolved cognition.

sections.title: Design, Cosmic Origins, and Natural Mechanisms
sections.rationale: This issue covers the competing explanations for functional complexity and cosmic origins, including divine agency, evolutionary processes, causal regress concerns, unsettled cosmology, and the permissibility of withholding conclusions while inquiry continues.

sections.title: Evidence, Falsifiability, and Explanatory Method
sections.rationale: This issue determines what could discriminate supernatural agency from natural or advanced-agent alternatives, whether theistic explanation supplies causal content, and whether either framework improperly fixes its conclusion regardless of possible observations.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Human Moral Status
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether moral truth and binding obligation require divine grounding or can arise from reason, reciprocity, flourishing, cooperation, moral psychology, and social inquiry, including the distinction between explaining moral beliefs and justifying them.

sections.title: Evil, Innocent Suffering, and Theistic Coherence
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether preventable innocent suffering conflicts with a perfectly good and powerful God, whether the objection presupposes objective moral standards, and whether a wider theistic account of suffering and death changes that conflict.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Christian theological commitments about an orderly and knowable creation motivated pioneers of the scientific revolution and contributed causally to modern science's emergence.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood remains the announced opening speaker and presents a sustained historical argument supported by attributed statements from named scientists.

response.rationale: This constructive supplies a historical causal contribution to the theistic case without answering an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a material subsidiary historical consideration but not the comparative motion as a whole.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical thesis is recoverable, but its causal scope across pioneers and the scientific revolution requires a more explicit comparative qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical dismissal of alternative historical explanations is stronger than the selected examples and excerpted comparison warrant.

charity.alternative: Christian identity may have accompanied scientific work without being a distinctive or necessary cause of modern science.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must distinguish causal theological motivation from background prevalence and compare non-Christian scientific traditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from named Christian pioneers and theological motivations to a broad causal contribution is intelligible but leaves a material causal-comparison bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named historical testimony supplies some support, yet representativeness, counterexamples, and independent causal comparison remain substantially underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly develops the subsidiary historical-origin bridge and sits near the top of that tier because the causal link is explicit.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions competing cultures and the dumb-luck alternative but weakens it without a sufficiently controlled historical comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span asks why Christians pioneered the scientific revolution, rejects the dumb-luck account, compares other civilizations, and elsewhere attributes statements to named scientists.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Extensive preventable suffering and death among innocent children conflicts with the joint claims that God is all-powerful and wholly good.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer announces his own arguments against God and presents the problem of evil in a continuous passage extending into the delivered boundary context.

response.rationale: This constructive states the logical-evidential tension and supplies quantitative examples of preventable child suffering without targeting an earlier move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops an indispensable problem-of-evil premise with concrete magnitude and preventability evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The triad and empirical class of innocent preventable suffering are clear, with the evidential rather than strict logical scope reasonably implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The suffering data strongly establish tension, though the compressed claim that all three propositions cannot coexist omits possible morally sufficient reasons.

charity.alternative: A perfectly good and powerful God could permit suffering for morally sufficient reasons unavailable to limited human observers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such a defense must address the scale, innocence, preventability, and apparently gratuitous distribution of the cited suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The incompatibility inference is strong as an evidential challenge but compresses the premise excluding morally sufficient divine reasons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific UNICEF-attributed mortality figures and preventable causes provide concrete representative support, with only the theological rival comparison underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly establishes the central problem-of-evil bridge through explicit claims about power, goodness, innocence, magnitude, and preventability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument fairly presses the strongest evidential facts, although it initially states the triad more categorically than a developed theodicy permits.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states the omnipotence-goodness-evil triad and cites daily and annual under-five mortality, emphasizing that the deaths are mainly preventable.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: A God hypothesis that treats favorable outcomes as confirmation while insulating every unfavorable outcome from disconfirmation lacks discriminating explanatory content.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening-statement turn and first-person presentation identify Michael Shermer as the speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive attacks the discriminating content of insulated divine explanations and illustrates its criterion through an irrefutable-assertion analogy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it sharply develops the falsifiability burden, though its application to every relevant theistic explanation is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional criticism is clear, but the span sometimes shifts from the insulated hypothesis under attack to the Christian worldview generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It correctly states a consequence of total insulation, though the claim that nothing could refute the relevant Christian explanation needs narrower scope.

charity.alternative: A theistic explanation may be indirectly testable through comparative expectations even if no single observation deductively refutes it.
charity.decisiveQualification: The proponent must specify asymmetric expectations or observations that lower the hypothesis's comparative support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If favorable and unfavorable outcomes are both absorbed, the conclusion about lost discrimination follows, with a bounded scope bridge to the actual hypothesis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quoted irrefutability claim and Sagan-style analogy illustrate the methodological defect, but the relevant theistic qualifications are not examined representatively.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is exceptionally direct contact with the subsidiary falsifiability bridge, reaching its exact concern about insulating qualifications and explanatory content.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a genuine insulation problem but gives limited attention to indirect or comparative confirmation rather than strict falsification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span asks what could refute the Christian causal explanation, answers that nothing can, calls it an assertion, and introduces Sagan's dragon as an illustration.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Theistic explanation need not infer God from temporary ignorance because it can appeal to established knowledge and the intelligible order of nature as a whole.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood remains the sole speaker and explicitly introduces Shermer's gaps objection before citing Christian criticism of that reasoning.

components.text: Show that the proposed theistic explanation is not merely an assertion insulated from evidence or disconfirmation.
Specify the positive knowledge or established order from which theistic explanation is inferred rather than a temporary gap.
Identify observations or comparative expectations capable of discriminating theism from rivals.

response.rationale: Wood directly denies relying on gaps and replaces ignorance with established knowledge and nature's overall order. That contacts the assertion and ignorance components, but it does not state a disconfirming observation or discriminating comparative expectation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a high partial answer because it contacts the central no-evidence premise but leaves the decisive discrimination demand unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The no-gaps distinction is recoverable, though 'all knowledge' and 'order as a whole' remain insufficiently specified as explanatory evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying the opening used no gaps is more confident than the excerpt's compressed positive warrant and absent rival comparison justify.

charity.alternative: An argument can avoid explicit appeals to ignorance yet still lack discriminating evidence and function as a gap explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Positive appeal to order must specify why that order favors divine agency over natural or other agent explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between ignorance-based and knowledge-based inference is valid, but the bridge from established order to divine agency remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical quotation supports Christian opposition to gap reasoning, yet it does not independently warrant the positive divine explanation or compare alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply attacks a central empirical-method demand by directly contesting the claim that theistic explanation is only an unsupported gap.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately rejects one version of the objection but does not fully engage the stronger explanatory-discrimination version.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span says the opening appealed to no gaps, characterizes God as God of all knowledge, and cites Henry Drummond's criticism of scanning nature for gaps.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: The question of who designed the designer does not defeat biological design reasoning because ordered functional composition is attributed to organisms but not likewise attributed to God.
moves.attributionBasis: Within Wood's rebuttal, the speaker explicitly identifies Shermer's designer question and answers it in his own sustained voice.

components.text: Explain how a God hypothesis gains discriminating evidential content rather than being protected from adverse outcomes.
Answer the narrower regress question by showing why the design property attributed to organisms need not be attributed to God.

response.rationale: The move answers a designer-regress objection, but the only earlier legal opposing target concerns unfalsifiability. The part-composition distinction is issue-bearing explanatory material without contacting that target's decisive discrimination demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it gives a coherent nearby methodological distinction but does not answer the selected earlier move's central requirement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The organism-God contrast is clear, but 'design,' 'complexity,' and the relevant divine simplicity condition are not held fully stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The regress distinction is plausible, but the stronger biological claim that no available natural means could compose the parts is insufficiently warranted.

charity.alternative: The designer challenge concerns explanatory complexity or information, not necessarily literal material parts arranged for a purpose.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show why a divine mind is explanatorily simpler or independently warranted, not merely non-composite.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The category distinction can block a simple identical regress, but it leaves the inference to design and the explanatory-complexity challenge materially open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies primarily on asserted limits of natural means and a conceptual contrast, without specific biological evidence or serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Despite weak response topology, the substance centrally advances the natural-explanations dispute over biological functional organization and designer regress.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response narrows the objection to material composition and therefore omits a decisive stronger interpretation about explanatory complexity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines biological complexity as ordered parts serving a purpose, asserts no available natural means, and asks whether that part-based reasoning applies to God.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: The problem of evil presupposes an objective moral law applicable even to God, creating a grounding burden for an atheist who uses suffering to argue against theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Wood's continuous rebuttal, signaled by his explicit transition to Shermer's problem-of-evil argument.

components.text: Justify the objective moral standard by which preventable child suffering counts against a perfectly good God.
Address the empirical magnitude, innocence, and preventability of the suffering cited as evidence against theism.
Explain how moral grounding removes rather than merely relocates the evidential tension among goodness, power, and suffering.

response.rationale: Wood contacts the metaethical standing of the objection by demanding a moral law and epistemic access to it. He does not address the suffering data or show that the grounding challenge defeats the internal evidential tension.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting a decisive presupposition, but it leaves the objection's empirical facts and internal critique largely untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding challenge is clear, but its scope shifts between an external atheist judgment and an internal critique of theism's own moral commitments.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that the objection makes no sense on atheism overstates what follows from the absence of theistic moral grounding.

charity.alternative: The problem of evil can be an internal critique using the theist's own claims about goodness without committing the critic to a complete moral ontology.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show that internal use of theistic goodness is illegitimate or that the cited suffering is compatible with that goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A critic asserting objective wrongness may owe a grounding account, but that does not by itself defeat an internal inconsistency or evidential argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is chiefly conceptual assertion and supplies no independent defense that atheism cannot support objective standards or moral knowledge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central problem-of-evil bridge by challenging the normative premise used to characterize the suffering as morally incompatible.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move largely treats the objection as an external atheist moral assertion and omits the strongest internal-critical formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt requires a moral standard binding on God and access to that law, then asserts that such claims make sense on Christianity but not atheism.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Scientific findings are publicly reproducible across religious cultures, whereas religious beliefs vary by place and time, so Christianity is not what validates scientific inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: This occurs after Wood's rebuttal and applause, in Shermer's resumed turn, with explicit references to theists, atheists, and Wood's science claim.

components.text: Show that Christian theology was a distinctive causal contributor to modern science rather than merely the religion of some pioneers.
Distinguish the historical origins of scientific institutions from the present cross-cultural validity of scientific findings.

response.rationale: Shermer contacts distinctiveness by showing that physics is available and reproducible across religious cultures. Present universality weakens necessity claims, but it does not directly settle the locked proposition's narrower historical causal-contribution claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that reaches the distinctive-validation premise but leaves the historical causation evidence substantially unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Cross-cultural reproducibility is clear, but the conclusion slides from what validates science now to what causally contributed to its emergence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Universal access shows Christianity is unnecessary for current practice, not that pioneers' theological attitudes were historically causally irrelevant.

charity.alternative: A tradition can causally help originate a universal method even though later practitioners need not share that tradition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response must separately evaluate historical motivation, institutional conditions, and counterfactual emergence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reproducibility premise supports universal accessibility, but the inference to historical irrelevance contains a substantial origin-versus-validity non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The India and common-physics examples strongly illustrate reproducibility, while evidence about the historical causal proposition is largely absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary scientific-history bridge, though its strongest evidence bears on validity rather than historical emergence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly rejects religious validation of results but underrepresents the stronger and narrower historical causal claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span notes that non-Christian physicists in India do the same physics and says the world's knowability is open to everyone regardless of religion.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Darwinian natural selection supplies a bottom-up mechanism by which apparently purposeful, complex biological organs can arise through cumulative gradual change without an intelligent designer.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer remains the uninterrupted speaker and explicitly turns to the appearance of design before naming Darwin and natural selection.

components.text: Address the claim that a part-composition regress does not apply to God in the same way it applies to organisms.
Provide an available natural mechanism capable of producing the ordered functional biological complexity used in the design inference.

response.rationale: Shermer supplies Darwinian cumulative selection as the missing natural mechanism and thereby attacks the biological-design premise. He does not engage Wood's primary category distinction concerning whether God has arranged constituent parts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it strongly answers a secondary biological premise but leaves the locked move's primary regress distinction untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative-selection proposition and its application to eyes and wings are clear, with ordinary implicit limits to evolved biological organs.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted role of cumulative natural selection in explaining adaptive biological complexity is proportionate to the mechanism described.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The bottom-up cumulative mechanism directly explains how apparently purposeful complex organs can arise from simpler variations without intentional assembly.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Eyes, wings, gradual structures, and natural selection provide specific mechanism-linked support, with only detailed evidence and rival boundary cases compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central natural-explanations bridge by supplying the relevant mechanism for apparent biological design.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own positive biological mechanism and does not materially interpret a live alternative beyond ordinary disagreement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies eyes and wings, credits Darwin with a bottom-up mechanism, and describes natural selection producing complex organs through simpler gradations over long periods.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Evidence for human makers of artifacts does not establish a cosmic maker; unresolved origins warrant testable inquiry and suspended judgment rather than an unsupported supernatural inference.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained Shermer turn explicitly answers Wood's garage-builder analogy and continues through his demand for empirical evidence of supernatural claims.

components.text: Answer the claim that biological part-composition reasoning need not generate an equivalent design regress for God.
Show that ordinary evidence for makers of artifacts does not transfer without further evidence to a maker of the universe.

response.rationale: The artifact-evidence distinction is highly relevant to design method and contacts an ancillary inference-to-maker issue. It does not address the primary organism-versus-God composition distinction in the legal target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer with substantial contrary evidence-method content but no contact with the target's decisive regress premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between observable human artifact makers and an inferred cosmic maker is stable, and suspension of judgment is clearly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately concludes that artifact analogies alone do not establish a cosmic maker and recommends continued inquiry rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: Order in nature might support agency abductively even without direct observation of the maker, as in some historical sciences.
charity.decisiveQualification: The inference still needs distinctive signatures, causal expectations, and comparison with natural mechanisms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential disanalogy between observed artifact production and cosmic origins coherently blocks a direct transfer of the maker inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Filming construction, contacting builders, and obtaining blueprints concretely support the artifact side, though cosmic rival evidence is only sketched.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central empirical-method bridge by demanding publicly accessible causal evidence before inferring a supernatural cosmic maker.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply allows the observed works claim but fairly insists that the artifact analogy lacks the independent maker evidence available for garages.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contrasts garages with the universe: human builders can be observed, contacted, filmed, and linked to blueprints, whereas comparable evidence for God is requested.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Because unguided natural selection selects for reproductive survival rather than truth, theism better explains the reliable cognition required for scientific knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood introduces Darwin and maintains the same uninterrupted rebuttal turn through his contrast between naturalistic and theistic expectations.

components.text: Explain why cross-cultural scientific success presupposes cognitive faculties capable of tracking truth rather than merely surviving.
Challenge whether natural selection's survival-directed mechanism is sufficient to explain generally reliable truth-directed cognition.
Supply discriminating evidence that theism predicts cognitive reliability better than natural alternatives.

response.rationale: Wood directly raises the reliability precondition beneath reproducibility and attacks selection's survival objective. The move does not establish that adaptive cognition is generally false or provide a developed likelihood comparison favoring theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive epistemic premise but leaves the positive comparative warrant and adaptive truth-tracking response unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability challenge is clear, but 'truth,' 'faculties,' and the range of cognition move from survival contexts to abstract science without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Selection for fitness does not by itself imply unreliable cognition, and the move lacks the extra premises required for a strong comparative conclusion.

charity.alternative: Accurate representation of many environmental features can be instrumentally valuable for survival, while cultural correction extends cognition beyond evolved defaults.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must show that fitness-preserving false beliefs dominate relevant alternatives or that scientific correction remains unexplained.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between fitness and truth identifies a possible underdetermination, but the inference to generally unreliable cognition is an unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Darwin's reported doubt supplies historical illustration, not representative empirical support that evolved cognition is unreliable or less expected than under theism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central scientific-intelligibility bridge by comparing naturalistic and theistic explanations of reliable cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invokes Darwin's doubt but does not adequately handle the strongest adaptive truth-tracking and cultural-correction account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether a Darwinian account of faculties licenses confidence in understanding the universe and invokes Darwin's own reported 'horrid doubt.'

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: A method that reclassifies every apparent divine act as advanced alien technology makes God's existence unknowable by design and cannot discriminate theological evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood expressly turns to Shermer's advanced-technology principle and develops the methodological objection until his rebuttal concludes.

components.text: Defend a skeptical method that requires discriminating evidence for a cosmic maker against the charge that it makes divine action unknowable by definition.
Explain what evidence could distinguish God from advanced agents or technology rather than merely redescribing apparent miracles.
Address the independent Darwinian mechanism for biological complexity.

response.rationale: Wood contacts the underdetermination problem by applying the advanced-technology principle to miracles and biological design, then argues that universal reclassification precludes knowledge. He does not supply positive discriminators or answer natural selection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer exposes a decisive methodological consequence but stops short of showing how theism can actually be discriminated from advanced-agent rivals.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological objection is recoverable and explicitly limits some applications, though 'God' and sufficiently advanced external agents remain partly conflated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical underdetermination is plausible, but unknowability follows only if every possible discriminator is excluded, which is not fully shown.

charity.alternative: Calling an event technologically reproducible does not rule out God; it withholds attribution until evidence distinguishes causal agents.
charity.decisiveQualification: The skeptical rule can remain defeasible if it permits distinctive evidence concerning scope, identity, intentions, or ultimate origin.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If every apparent divine act is automatically redescribed as alien technology, divine attribution is excluded; the universal premise, however, is not fully established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument uses illuminating hypotheticals about miracles and biology but supplies little evidence that the opponent's actual method excludes all discriminators.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary burden-method bridge by asking what could distinguish divine agency from advanced-agent explanations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move sees the danger of permanent reclassification but treats a cautious underdetermination principle as closer to definitional exclusion than necessary.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span applies the advanced-technology principle to biological design and miracles, questions its application to a universe, and presents the resulting attribution problem.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Successful measurement, prediction, and spacecraft navigation provide empirical evidence that evolved human faculties increasingly represent and track an external reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Shermer the rebuttal, and he directly addresses the preceding natural-selection challenge in one continuous passage.

components.text: Show that evolved cognition can track external truth well enough for reliable scientific measurement, prediction, and intervention.
Explain why selection for survival can favor sufficiently accurate representation rather than merely useful false belief.
Address whether successful prediction can distinguish naturalistic cognition from a theistic explanation of cognition.

response.rationale: Shermer directly supplies spacecraft navigation and improving measurement as empirical evidence of reliable access to reality. He establishes observed reliability but does not fully explain its evolutionary production or compare theism's prediction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a high partial answer because it contacts the decisive reliability claim with empirical success while leaving the etiological and comparative components open.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to improving capabilities for measuring, detecting, and predicting external reality rather than perfect cognition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated successful prediction and navigation warrant confidence in domain-specific cognitive reliability, with improvement acknowledging fallibility.

charity.alternative: Scientific success can show instrumentally reliable outputs without explaining why unguided evolution produced truth-directed faculties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response establishes reliability empirically but must separately answer the evolutionary and comparative explanatory challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Successful precise navigation and prediction are strong abductive evidence that instruments and corrected human cognition track relevant external structures.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Spacecraft reaching Mars and improving measurement provide concrete success evidence, though broader cognitive domains and evolutionary mechanisms remain unexamined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central scientific-intelligibility bridge by empirically defending the reliability of evolved and scientifically corrected cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: Shermer accurately rejects global unreliability with concrete success while leaving, rather than caricaturing, the deeper origin question compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites spacecraft navigation to Mars and progressively improved measurement, detection, and prediction as outcomes that would fail without reality-tracking senses.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Biological wiring and social teaching can causally explain moral convictions but cannot establish that the conduct condemned by those convictions is objectively wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows Shermer's question to Wood and continues Wood's first-person comparison of theistic and naturalistic moral explanations.

components.text: Treat empirical causal evidence and suspended judgment as sufficient methodological answers to normative moral justification.
Infer normative truth from the successful causal functioning or reliability of evolved cognitive and social dispositions.

response.rationale: Although the legal earlier targets are methodological and epistemic rather than an explicit morality move, Wood expressly diagnoses a cause-versus-justification error: hardwiring or teaching may explain belief formation but does not entail objective wrongness. That defeating consequence preserves the legitimate empirical question while denying its normative sufficiency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it clearly identifies the is-to-ought inferential failure and states why causal origins cannot complete normative justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between causal explanation of a belief and justification of its objective content is explicit and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately limited: causal hardwiring or social teaching alone does not logically establish objective moral truth.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic moral justification may appeal to reasons and facts about welfare, agency, and reciprocity, not merely the causes of belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: The diagnostic defeat applies only to causal explanations offered without an independent normative bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cause-versus-justification distinction is explicit and valid: explaining why a conviction occurs does not entail that its content is objectively true.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hardwiring and social-teaching examples effectively demonstrate underdetermination, though rival secular justificatory premises are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central secular-morality bridge by requiring a normative warrant beyond evolved feelings or conditioned beliefs.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly isolates a genuine inferential error, though its broader framing risks understating reason-based naturalistic moral theories.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span asks about the status of a moral belief under naturalism and contrasts hardwiring or social teaching with whether the condemned conduct is actually wrong.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Love, promise-keeping, reciprocity, social cooperation, and the survival and flourishing of sentient beings provide secular reasons for binding moral conduct without divine commands.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Shermer's closing, and the speaker answers Wood directly while developing Shermer's previously stated secular moral criterion.

components.text: Supply secular normative reasons, rather than merely causal origins, for treating conduct as right, wrong, or binding.
Explain why survival and flourishing of sentient beings should function as an authoritative moral standard.
Show how human reasoning can discover and improve moral principles under a naturalistic account.

response.rationale: Shermer moves beyond causal wiring by invoking reciprocity, promise-keeping, suffering, cooperation, and reasoned principles. These are candidate secular reasons, but the foundational authority of flourishing is asserted rather than fully justified.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This high partial answer contacts the decisive demand for reasons while leaving the metaethical bridge from flourishing facts to binding obligation compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The secular standard is recoverable, but 'work,' 'flourishing,' and 'binding' span prudential, social, and moral senses without full differentiation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited considerations plausibly support many duties, though claiming binding morality without a further authority premise slightly exceeds the warrant.

charity.alternative: A flourishing criterion may explain desirable outcomes yet still presuppose that flourishing ought to be promoted.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response must justify the normative priority and resolve conflicts among flourishing, autonomy, reciprocity, and suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reciprocity and sentient welfare coherently generate many action-guiding reasons, but the bridge to categorical objective obligation remains materially implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete considerations about suffering, promises, cooperation, and social progress support the account, while conflicting cases and foundational warrants are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central secular-morality bridge through flourishing, reciprocity, cooperation, reason, and sentient suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move provides substantive secular reasons but does not squarely acknowledge the strongest foundational is-to-ought objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds discovered moral principles in sentient survival and flourishing, invokes Bentham's suffering criterion, and the larger locked proposition includes love, promises, and reciprocity.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Biblical creation and modern scientific findings can be reconciled through Christian traditions that use observation and experiment to discover how God ordered nature.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question explicitly addresses Wood, and the response draws on his earlier discussion of the scientific revolution and theistic scientific method.

components.text: Answer the secular claim that flourishing, suffering, reciprocity, and reasoning can justify moral conduct without divine commands.
Show that Christian creation commitments can encourage observation and experiment without dictating scientific results.
Reconcile biblical creation claims with the specific Darwinian mechanism and relevant scientific findings.

response.rationale: The only legal primary target is the prior morality reply, which this origins answer does not contact. It provides relevant contrary material to the earlier science-history dispute by presenting a Christian rationale for empirical inquiry, but does not address Darwinian details.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it supplies meaningful issue-bearing historical-method material but wholly misses the legal primary morality demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empirical-inquiry compatibility claim is clear, but the broader reconciliation of biblical creation with modern findings is only indirectly supported.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that Christian traditions can support observation and experiment is appropriately modest and supported by the stated methodological example.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If scripture does not specify contingent natural operations, observation and experiment coherently become the means of discovering those operations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical methodological example supports compatibility, but the claimed reconciliation with modern origins science lacks specific scriptural and scientific comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally attacks the natural-explanations implication that biblical creation necessarily displaces empirical investigation of natural order.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span explains a compatible Christian empirical method without materially interpreting or attacking a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span says contingent natural operations cannot be known by necessity and therefore must be discovered through observation and experiment into how nature works.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Appeals to flourishing and autonomy do not by themselves justify those norms, whereas creation in God's image supplies humans with a distinctive moral status.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Wood one minute, and the response continues through the locked lookahead until the moderator announces the next question.

components.text: Justify why survival, flourishing, autonomy, or suffering should possess binding normative authority rather than being asserted starting points.
Explain why humans receive distinctive or equal moral status within a broader class of sentient beings.
Defend creation in God's image as a non-circular and independently warranted ground of moral status.

response.rationale: Wood directly challenges the undefended normative starting point and the preference for humans among sentient beings, then offers divine image as a status ground. The positive grounding premise itself receives little defense.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a high partial answer because it contacts both foundational authority and status, while leaving the positive divine-image warrant underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-part challenge and proposed status ground are recoverable, with the theological meaning and extent of divine image left implicitly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The critique of undefended foundations is well fitted, but presenting divine image as a sufficient ground requires further theological and normative warrants.

charity.alternative: Sentience can ground equal consideration of suffering without implying that humans alone matter or that all sentient interests are identical.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection must distinguish species preference from morally relevant differences in agency, relationships, and capacities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for justification and the status problem are coherent, but the move does not complete the bridge from divine image to objective obligation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The secular starting-point quotation supports the critique, while the positive divine-image account is asserted without independent support or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central moral-grounding bridge by distinguishing normative status from asserted flourishing and sentience criteria.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a real status question but frames the secular account as preferring humans more straightforwardly than its sentience criterion requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls autonomy and flourishing undefended principles, asks why humans should be preferred among sentient beings, and the locked proposition offers divine image as the answer.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: The consoling prospect of reunion after death does not answer suffering unless it is true, and incompatible religious afterlife accounts intensify the need for supporting evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer directly addresses the audience member's repeated afterlife claim, uses Shermer's skeptical burden-of-proof reasoning, and contrasts Christian and Islamic beliefs.

components.text: Answer the claim that divine image provides distinctive human moral status and that secular flourishing lacks comparable authority.
Require evidence for the theistic afterlife premise used to place earthly suffering in a wider moral context.
Address whether empirical inquiry can establish one specific religious afterlife account over incompatible alternatives.

response.rationale: The move does not contact the legal primary target's divine-image grounding claim. It is nevertheless issue-bearing and directly challenges an emerging afterlife response by demanding evidence and invoking incompatible religious accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong relevant nonanswer: it develops an important evidential objection but does not answer the selected earlier morality move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional point is precise: consolation bears argumentative weight only if the afterlife claim is true and sufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Demanding evidential support before using a disputed afterlife premise is proportionate, and acknowledged lack of direct access is epistemically appropriate.

charity.alternative: An afterlife need only be epistemically possible to block a strict logical contradiction between God and suffering.
charity.decisiveQualification: Possibility may preserve coherence but cannot by itself neutralize the evidential weight of suffering or establish consolation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A disputed afterlife cannot answer an evidential objection unless supported, and incompatible accounts coherently increase the specificity burden.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious plurality provides a concrete underdetermination point, though the move does not compare the actual evidential cases for the different accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally attacks the theistic evil-coherence bridge by challenging the truth and specificity of the proposed eschatological premise.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly distinguishes comforting possibility from truth and appropriately emphasizes evidence when the premise carries evidential rather than merely logical weight.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span repeatedly asks how the afterlife claim is known, rejects a burden to disprove heaven, and notes that many incompatible versions of the afterlife exist.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Theism remains coherent amid suffering because death need not end a person's story and an afterlife can change the total context of apparently final earthly harms.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly interprets the audience member's theistic point and frames it through the problem of evil, matching Wood's defense of theism.

components.text: Explain how an afterlife can change the problem-of-evil assessment despite the demand for evidence and competing afterlife accounts.
Show how continuation after death addresses the magnitude, preventability, and innocence of earthly child suffering.
Provide discriminating evidence for the afterlife rather than using it as an insulating possibility.

response.rationale: Wood contacts the contextual role of an afterlife by explaining that death may not be the end and thus earthly harm may not be final. He does not answer Shermer's truth, evidence, or religious-specificity demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the legitimate contextual consequence but leaves the primary evidential qualification and original suffering facts unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move is explicitly modal and contextual: an afterlife can provide explanatory resources rather than conclusively proving that suffering is justified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The repeated 'maybe' and contextual framing accurately limit the conclusion to possible coherence rather than probability or certainty.

charity.alternative: Continuation after death may compensate a victim without justifying why preventable suffering was permitted in the first place.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compensation and non-finality do not alone supply a morally sufficient reason for permitting the harm.

logicalCoherence.rationale: An afterlife can alter total-harm assessment and block finality assumptions, but it does not by itself reconcile permission of preventable suffering.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion is supported only as a conditional possibility; no evidence establishes the afterlife or a mechanism connecting it to moral justification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central evil-coherence bridge by supplying theism's eschatological context for apparently final earthly harms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly adds a neglected temporal context but does not engage the decisive distinction between later compensation and antecedent justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says theists deny that death ends a child's story and cautiously proposes that this broader context supplies explanatory resources for the problem of evil.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Current cosmology does not require a divine first cause because quantum events may be uncaused and the universe may have deeper or eternal physical antecedents, while its origin remains unsettled.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is addressed to Shermer, and the answer explicitly appeals to contemporary physics, alternative cosmological models, and epistemic uncertainty in his established voice.

components.text: Show that empirical inquiry into origins does not presently require the biblical or divine explanation offered as a compatible framework.
Offer possible physical antecedents or uncaused events that prevent a simple first-cause regress from selecting God.
Preserve provisional judgment under underdetermined origin hypotheses rather than excluding theism by definition.
Address the evidential role of an afterlife in the problem of evil.

response.rationale: Shermer directly reframes origins as an unsettled empirical question and offers quantum and eternal-antecedent possibilities. This contacts the inquiry and regress demands without claiming that the alternatives are established, though it does not refute mere compatibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This full answer addresses the empirical replacement demand and its uncertainty, with a bounded gap concerning extrapolation from quantum events to cosmic origins.

precisionFindings.rationale: The provisional alternatives and unsettled conclusion are explicit, though 'uncaused' at quantum and cosmological levels may not carry identical meanings.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The overall provisional force is apt, but saying quantum events are truly uncaused and extending that model to the universe is somewhat stronger than shown.

charity.alternative: Quantum indeterminacy within a physical framework may not explain why any physical reality exists or remove a metaphysical first-cause question.
charity.decisiveQualification: The alternatives block a quick scientific inference to God but do not by themselves answer the ultimate contingency question.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple live physical possibilities coherently undercut necessity claims, though analogy from subatomic events to cosmic origin leaves one material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Quantum experiments and contemporary models provide relevant support, but the cosmic extrapolation and eternal antecedent possibilities remain provisional and selectively developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central natural-explanations bridge through provisional physical mechanisms and disciplined suspension of judgment about origins.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move appropriately withholds a final conclusion and presents alternatives, while leaving the strongest metaphysical version largely outside its empirical scope.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt appeals to experimentally supported quantum events described as uncaused, suggests the universe's beginning may be analogous, and considers an infinitely old physical reality.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Rejecting absolute or religious moral ontology does not entail relativism because social science can discover real truths about human nature, moral dispositions, and behavior-regulating institutions.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows a question explicitly addressed to Shermer about his book and develops his characteristic naturalistic account through human nature and social-scientific study.

components.text: Address whether an afterlife changes the moral assessment of preventable innocent suffering under theism.
Show that rejecting divine-image ontology need not collapse morality into individual or cultural relativism.
Distinguish discovering empirical truths about human moral life from justifying objective normative obligations.

response.rationale: The move does not contact the legal primary afterlife target. It provides substantial contrary material to earlier moral-grounding moves by defending discoverable social-scientific truths, but it does not complete the cause-to-justification bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it strongly addresses relativism and empirical discovery but misses the primary target and the central normative-authority demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-relativist thesis is clear, but 'objective truths' shifts between descriptive facts about humans and normative truths about what ought to be done.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Social science can discover descriptive regularities, but the move overstates their sufficiency for objective moral obligation without a normative bridge.

charity.alternative: The theistic objection can accept descriptive social-scientific truths while denying that they entail categorical moral duties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response must connect empirical findings to justified normative standards rather than merely label both kinds of claim truths.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Rejecting religious absolutes does not entail relativism, but the inference from social-scientific discovery to objective morality contains a substantial missing normative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Psychology, cognitive science, economics, and historical social research support descriptive claims, while their warrant for binding moral conclusions remains underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central secular-morality bridge by locating moral inquiry in empirical truths about human nature, dispositions, and institutions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly rejects crude relativism but materially underanswers the strongest descriptive-versus-normative distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites social science, psychology, cognitive science, economics, human nature, and society as disciplines discovering real truths relevant to moral behavior.
